Here is the one-time step for each. macOS Windows Linux Infinite is an ad-hoc signed community app, so macOS Gatekeeper asks for a one-time confirmation on first launch. 1 Double-click the app Drag Infinite.app to Applications and double-click it. macOS says it is from an unverified developer. 2 Open anyway Open System Settings, Privacy & Security , scroll to Security, and click Open Anyway . 3 Or one line in Terminal Remove the quarantine flag instantly: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Infinite.app The Windows build is a portable folder: no installer, nothing written to your registry. It is unsigned, so Windows warns once on first launch. Most PCs need the Intel / AMD (x64) build. On a Snapdragon X or other ARM laptop take the ARM64 build instead (check Settings, System, About, System type if unsure). 1 Unblock the ZIP Right-click the ZIP, choose Properties , tick Unblock , then OK . Then extract it. Doing this first saves you a prompt for every file inside. 2 Run anyway Run Infinite.exe . If SmartScreen appears, click More info , then Run anyway . Keep the folder together: Infinite.exe loads its assets from beside itself. 3 Opening patches Patches save as .infinite files. Right-click one, Open with, Choose another app , pick Infinite.exe and tick Always . Dragging a patch onto the canvas works with no setup. Infinite ships as one portable AppImage . It bundles the static AppImage runtime, so you do not need libfuse2 . Needs x86_64, glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, Fedora 38+ or similar) and OpenGL 3.2 via X11 or XWayland. 1 Make it executable Download Infinite-x86_64.AppImage , then: chmod +x Infinite-x86_64.AppImage 2 Run it Double-click it, or run it from a terminal. Philosophy of Infinite: creative software built for flow
Why Infinite is a node graph, how it protects flow state in art and music making, how machines should work with people, and the design principles behind it.

Philosophy . Why Infinite exists . A graph, because ideas connect . Anything patches into anything . Flow, with a machine that follows you . Free, for everyone . Who it's for . Philosophy Why Infinite exists One canvas for pictures, sound and code, so an idea can travel from your head to the screen or the speakers without switching tools. A graph, because ideas connect A patch is a map of how things connect, and ideas connect in more than a line. Anything patches into anything Each node does one job and each cable says what feeds what. A sound can move a picture and a picture can move a sound. Who it's for Artists Musicians VJs Creative coders Developers Why is Infinite a node-based program? A patch is a map of how things connect, and ideas connect in more than a line. Each node does one job and each cable says what feeds what, so you can see the whole shape of a piece at once, and anything can patch into anything: a sound can move a picture and a picture can move a sound. What does flow state mean for music and art software? Flow is the state where doing and thinking are the same act. Software breaks it with dialogs, loading, deep menus and delay. Infinite keeps controls live while a patch plays, keeps pictures, sound, 3D and code in one graph, and lets any knob be moved by a controller, an LFO, an envelope or the audio itself. Who is Infinite for? Artists, musicians, VJs, creative coders and technologists, and developers who want to render from a text file or give an AI agent the same tools. Each has its own page on this site. Is Infinite free? Yes. Infinite is free to download for macOS, Windows and Linux. The source is on GitHub under the MIT licence, and the binary is GPLv3 by default because it bundles VST3 hosting. Can AI agents use Infinite? Yes. Patches are plain text, and Infinite can render them headless from the command line, from a Python SDK, or through nine MCP tools. The person decides what is kept.

Keep reading . on this page The architecture: how AI agents interact with Infinite One-command installation for Claude, Cursor and Windsurf Manual MCP Configuration Using the Python SDK Embedding interactive widgets in generated sites AI coding assistants (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Antigravity, Devin) are exceptionally good at writing code, but historically poor at producing interactive music and real-time 3D visuals. Desktop DAWs and visual engines require manual mouse interactions, proprietary project files, and heavy graphical interfaces that agents cannot operate. Infinite bridges this gap by exposing its entire C++20 engine through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and a dedicated Python SDK . The architecture: how AI agents interact with Infinite [Claude / Cursor / Antigravity] | (JSON-RPC stdio) v [tools/mcp/infinite_mcp.py] | (Headless C++ Engine) v [Audio .wav / Still .png / Video .mp4] Every action is deterministic and headless: The AI agent generates a formula or patch. The MCP server pipes it into ./Infinite --validate . If valid, the C++ engine renders frames or synthesizes 24-bit audio in milliseconds. The output file path and spectral analysis return to the AI agent context. One-command installation for Claude, Cursor and Windsurf You can automatically wire up Infinite across all your AI assistants with a single command: npx -y infinite-engine init It adds the infinite MCP server to Claude Desktop, Cursor and Windsurf, but only for apps that are already installed. It keeps a backup of each file it changes, and leaves a config alone if it contains comments. Add --dry-run to see what it would do first. The Infinite app itself must be installed; set INFINITE_BIN to its path if it is not found. Manual MCP Configuration If you prefer to configure your assistants manually: { "mcpServers": { "infinite": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "infinite-engine", "serve"] } } } Now your assistant has nine tools (ask the server for tools/list to see their exact schemas): infinite_render_video : renders a patch to MP4. infinite_render_field_pixel : renders a still frame from a Field Pixel preset. infinite_synthesize_field_synth : renders a synth voice to audio. infinite_synthesize_field_notes : builds an algorithmic note sequence. infinite_process_field_effect : runs audio through a Field effect. infinite_render_sketch3d : renders a 3D sketch written in JavaScript. infinite_render_field_primitive : maps a formula to a 3D surface. infinite_render_field_modifier : deforms a mesh with a Field modifier. infinite_validate_patch : checks a patch for errors. The Python SDK also ships an MCP server ( tools/mcp/infinite_mcp.py , from a checkout) with its own tool names. Infinite headless engine lets AI agents write text patches, inspect signals, and render music, pictures and 3D from the command line.

Keep reading . on this page Why a text patch suits an agent The loop an agent follows Music: notes, a synth and a measurement Art: a picture written as a formula Sound that drives the picture 3D: a shape, a camera, a light and Render 3D What to ask for Limits to know Try it An AI agent that can run shell commands can make music, pictures and 3D with Infinite, because the engine runs headless. The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool. It reads a plain-text patch and writes stills, video and audio, with no window and no mouse. A patch is text, so an agent such as Claude can write it, check it, listen to it and fix it in a loop. This post shows that loop, then three small patches: a sound, a picture and a 3D scene. It builds on the headless render walkthrough and the Headless User Guide . Why a text patch suits an agent Most creative tools hide their state behind a window. An agent can only guess at what a click did. An Infinite patch is different in four ways: It is text. A patch is a list of node , cable , mod and expr lines in a .inf file. An agent writes it the way it writes code, and it diffs cleanly in version control. The engine explains itself. Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with defaults, ranges and dropdown options, so the agent never has to guess a name or a range. Errors are specific. --validate reports every problem with a line number and a hint that names the nearest valid key. Results are machine readable. The last line printed is one JSON object with ok , files , warnings and errors , and the exit code says whether the patch loaded, was refused or failed to render. The output is also deterministic: the same patch gives the same frames and the same samples, so an agent can change one thing and trust that any difference came from that change. The loop an agent follows The Headless User Guide gives the order, and it works as a prompt for an agent as it stands: Describe. Ask the engine for the node's controls with --describe . Do not guess. Write the smallest patch that could work. Leave every control you do not change at its default. Validate with --validate until the exit code is 0. Explain with --explain , which prints the graph that was actually built. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch, so the agent compares this against what you asked for. Look and listen. --frame draws stills and --audio-summary describes the sound as numbers. Fix one thing at a time and go back to step 3. Render the final file with --render . Infinite ships this loop as an agent skill, infinite-patch-authoring , written for AI coding agents. Point your agent at it and at the Headless User Guide, then describe what you want. Music: notes, a synth and a measurement This is the smallest audio patch that ships with Infinite. A random note generator plays a Wavetable synth into an Audio Out. infinite-patch 1 node 1 Notes Random Note Generator id notes end node 2 Synths Wavetable id synth end node 3 Utility Audio Out id speakers end note synth 0 notes aud speakers 0 synth An agent cannot hear, so it measures. --audio-summary writes loudness, peaks, clipping, silence, a spectrum and a tempo guess to a JSON file, and --wav keeps the audio. Infinite --validate music.inf Infinite --audio-summary music.inf summary.json --wav music.wav --duration 8 Two warnings are worth teaching your agent to react to. W_SILENT means no sound reached an Audio Out, so check that notes reach the synth. W_CLIPPING means samples hit full scale, so lower a gain or add a Limiter. By connecting live sound analysis to GPU fragment programs, visual elements can pulse, distort, and morph in tight synchronisation with incoming music. In Infinite , shaders and audio live on the same canvas. Rather than relying on separate applications communicating over Spout or NDI with variable latency, the audio engine and the GPU render pipeline share memory and clock timing. This article explains how to build custom audio-reactive GLSL shaders using the Field Pixel node, map fast Fourier transform frequency bands to shader uniforms, and maintain solid frame rates during live performance. The architecture of audio-reactive shaders A conventional graphics pipeline draws frames by calculating colour values for each pixel coordinate on the screen. In standard GLSL fragment shaders, coordinates arrive as normalized screen positions ranging from zero to one. To make these coordinates move with music, the shader requires numerical inputs that reflect acoustic energy across time. In Infinite, this bridge is formed by two native nodes: Audio Analyze : An audio-rate sink that continuously computes an 8-band FFT spectrum, root-mean-square amplitude, and transient onset energy from any incoming sound signal. Field Pixel : A GPU shader node that compiles high-level Field kernel code directly into GLSL 150 fragment programs, exposing declared parameters as modulatable pins. Because the audio engine runs on dedicated real-time worker threads while the rendering engine operates on the main display loop, modulation values pass through lock-free ring buffers. This prevents audio dropouts or graphics stutter, ensuring that modulation data reaches shader uniforms at full monitor refresh rates. Extracting frequency bands with Audio Analyze Before writing shader logic, the patch needs an acoustic signal. You can route an audio file, a live microphone input, a synthesizer such as Analog , or a third-party VST3 instrument into an Audio Analyze node. The Audio Analyze node inspects incoming 48 kHz audio buffers and separates the frequency spectrum into distinct musical bands: low : Energy below 250 Hz, capturing kick drums and sub-bass weight. mid : Energy between 250 Hz and 4 kHz, covering vocals, synth leads, and snare bodies. high : Energy above 4 kHz, capturing hi-hats, cymbals, and transient attacks. level : The overall instantaneous RMS volume of the combined signal. Each of these four measurements appears as an output pin on the node. When a cable is drawn from one of these pins to a shader parameter, Infinite updates the corresponding uniform before each frame render. Writing GPU shaders in the Field Pixel node The Field Pixel node allows you to author shader kernels directly in the node inspector. The Field compiler translates bare mathematical expressions into vectorised GLSL instructions. Keep reading . on this page From nuclear accelerators to world rhythms The closed-form integer Bresenham formula Implementing Euclidean algorithms in Field Notes Polyrhythms, phase shifting, and polymetre Simultaneous audio transients and 3D visual geometry Creative applications in your music A Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithm distributes a fixed number of active musical pulses as evenly as possible across a discrete timeline of metric steps. First identified in computer science by E. Bjorklund in 2003 for timing neutron accelerators at Los Alamos, and brought into music theory by Godfried Toussaint in 2005, Euclidean rhythms revealed a startling truth: the mathematical distribution of pulses on a circle generates the foundational rhythmic structures of traditional music worldwide. In modern modular synthesis and creative coding environments like Infinite , Euclidean sequencers provide an elegant alternative to static step grids. Because the pattern emerges directly from two integer parameters, pulse count and step length, composers can morph complex groove structures live without editing step arrays by hand. Here is how the mathematics work, how to implement the algorithm in a single line of procedural code, and how to patch Euclidean triggers into synthesizers and 3D geometry simultaneously. Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithm diagram showing geometric hit distributions and modular node patching From nuclear accelerators to world rhythms The core challenge of rhythmic distribution can be stated simply: given $n$ available steps in a bar and $k$ active beats, how can we space the beats so the interval between any two consecutive hits differs by at most one step? Bjorklund originally developed an iterative algorithm based on Euclid's greatest common divisor method. Starting with a set of $k$ ones (active hits) and $n - k$ zeros (rests), the algorithm repeatedly distributes the smaller group into remainder sequences until no division remains. When applied to musical intervals, Toussaint observed that this mechanical reduction produces virtually every major non-Western and folk timeline pattern: E(3, 8) produces [X . . X . . X .] , the Cuban tresillo and Caribbean habanera rhythm. E(5, 8) produces [X . X X . X X .] , the Cuban cinquillo and Spanish tango. E(5, 12) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X .] , the Venda clapping pattern from South Africa. E(7, 12) produces [X . X . X X . X . X . X] , the West African bell pattern (Bembe), which is also geometrically isomorphic to the diatonic major scale on a twelve-tone chromatic circle. E(5, 16) produces [X . . X . . X . . . X . . X . .] , the Brazilian bossa nova necklace. E(7, 16) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X . . X . .] , a fundamental Brazilian samba rhythm. Because each pattern can be rotated around the circular step circle, a single pair of integers yields multiple distinct syncopations simply by advancing the starting step index. The closed-form integer Bresenham formula While Bjorklund's recursive array partitioning works well for static sequence generation, running recursive string manipulations inside a real-time audio thread or graphics shader is inefficient. Fortunately, Euclidean distribution can be expressed in closed form as a one-dimensional Bresenham line-drawing algorithm. Imagine drawing a continuous line from coordinate (0, 0) to (n, k) on a 2D integer grid. Each time the line crosses an integer threshold on the vertical axis, an active hit occurs. For any discrete step index $s \in [0, n - 1]$, the state of the trigger is calculated directly by comparing two consecutive floor evaluations: on(s) = floor((s + 1) * k / n) - floor(s * k / n) This mathematical identi

Field: write a kernel, the node decides where it runs
Field is the language built into Infinite. One kernel can become a shader, a geometry deformer or an audio effect, depending on the node it lives in.

Keep reading . on this page One idea: a kernel run once per element The Field nodes Knobs that become pins Why a language, not another plugin format Most nodes do one fixed thing. A Blur node blurs and a Delay node delays. Creative work often needs something in between, so Infinite includes Field , a kernel language for shaders, geometry and audio: a small language for writing what a node does. One idea: a kernel run once per element A Field node runs your kernel once for every element of its domain, forever. The domain is chosen by the node, not by you: col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5) // once per pixel, on the GPU: a shader P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 // once per point in a mesh: a geometry deformer out = in * gain // once per audio sample: a DSP effect You never declare a backend. The same way of thinking covers pictures, shapes and sound. The Field nodes Node Domain What it does Field Pixel pixel Per-pixel kernel compiled to GLSL, with state cells for feedback Field Modifier element Per-vertex kernel over existing geometry Field Primitive element Generates point geometry such as spirals, lattices and torus knots Field Effect sample Per-sample audio effect with in , out , state and param Field Synth sample A polyphonic synth voice driven by freq and gate Field Notes sample Sends notes with note(pitch, vel, len) and reads the transport Field Graph graph Runs at edit time and builds real nodes and cables Knobs that become pins A kernel can declare parameters in its own code, and each one becomes a real input on the node: param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99] state float z = 0 z += (in - z) * cutoff out = z That is a one-pole low-pass filter. The cutoff pin can be wired to an LFO, a MIDI knob or the output of an Audio Analyze node like any other control, and it survives save and load. Why a language, not another plugin format A kernel is short enough to read in one go and to share as a text file. The Library has a growing set of free Field devices to start from, and the language reference is available as a PDF manual . Keep reading . on this page What Infinite does well for this job Where TouchDesigner is stronger A quick way to judge it Bringing a shader over If you make audio-reactive visuals, you have probably met TouchDesigner. It is powerful, mature and has a large community. It is also a visual tool first: sound comes in through operators, and a full music setup usually means a second program next to it. Infinite starts from the other side. It is a DAW and a visual tool on one canvas, free and open source. This page is a practical comparison, including the places where TouchDesigner is the better pick. What Infinite does well for this job Audio and visuals share a canvas. Synths, sequencers and plugins sit next to shaders and 3D, wired with cables. There is no OSC bridge to set up. Audio analysis is a node. Audio Analyze gives an 8-band FFT and onset detection that you can wire to any control. It hosts plugins. AU (macOS) and VST3 (macOS, Windows, Linux) plugins load into the graph, and their parameters can be modulated by visuals. It is free and open source. No licence tier, and the source is on GitHub . Video out to other tools. Syphon (macOS), Spout (Windows) and NDI carry the picture to a projector tool or a streaming setup. Where TouchDesigner is stronger It has been around for years, so the amount of tutorials, forum answers and shared networks is far larger. Python scripting and a deep set of operators cover installations and data work that Infinite does not aim at. Many venues and teams already have TouchDesigner in their pipeline. If your show depends on that ecosystem, stay there. If you want sound and picture designed together, with a synth and a shader in the same patch, Infinite is worth an afternoon. We publish the numbers that are good for us and the ones that are not. The full report is on the benchmarks page , with a PDF and the raw data as JSON. How we tested Everything ran on a base MacBook Air with an Apple M2 and 8 GB of memory, on macOS, between 12 and 17 October 2026. That is the cheapest model on purpose: if it is fast there, it is fast on yours. Nothing was measured on Windows or Linux. The tests treat every product as a black box. Notes or a test signal go in, and what comes out is measured. Competitor plugins run inside Infinite's own plugin host, with default settings and no hand-picked presets, and the same code measures them as measures Infinite's own nodes. The tools are in the repository under tools/re-survey , so you can repeat any of it. The good news Launch: 0.34 seconds from launch to first frame. Opening a 400-node patch takes 6 ms. Footprint: 244 MB of memory with the app open and idle, and a 45 MB download. That is less memory than Ableton Live (672 MB), Blender (693 MB), Bitwig (1,392 MB) and TouchDesigner (1,396 MB) in the same idle test. Synth accuracy: The Wavetable synth has a worst pitch error of 0.2 cents across the keyboard. Vital and Serum 2 measure the same. Off-note energy stays between about -81 and -85 dB, even at the top of the keyboard where cheap synths alias. Synth cost: The Wavetable synth uses 1.45 ms of CPU per second of audio for each voice. Vital uses 2.82 ms and Serum 2 uses 3.23 ms. Video export: On matched test scenes, Infinite exported ProRes 4444 at 170 frames a second at 720p and 44 at 4K. Blender managed 1.6 and 0.5. These are different renderers, so this compares throughput, not image style. Plugins: 97.6 % of the plugins installed on the test machine load and pass audio in Infinite's plugin host. Live use: zero audio dropouts and zero missed screen refreshes in the standard live-performance test. Where Infinite is behind We list these on the report as below target: Idle CPU: With nothing loaded, Infinite sits at 12.3 % of one core. Logic, Blender and Vital sit under 4 %. Built-in effects: The EQ, Limiter, Drive and Chorus cost more CPU than the plugin equivalents. Instancing: 10,000 instanced objects cost 3.1 ms a frame in Infinite and 1.3 ms in Blender. Heavy projector scenes: The heaviest test (four 4K videos, three output windows, a camera and Syphon at once) drops frames. Normal and 1080p scenes do not. Default levels: Reverb, Delay, Chorus and Flanger come out louder than they go in at their default settings. What the numbers do not say One laptop is one data point. The comparisons are about throughput and cost under a fixed test, not about taste: a faster export does not make a better picture, and equal pitch accuracy does not make two synths sound alike. Windows and Linux numbers will come later. Check it yourself Everything is repeatable. In practice, embedding real-time generative computer graphics on the web usually means pulling in large third-party runtime bundles, wrangling WebAudio permission policies, managing asset loading cascades, and debugging WebGL canvas resize glitches across mobile viewports. Infinite approaches web graphics from a different perspective. Because Infinite compiles procedural fragment shaders, JavaScript sketches, and per-sample audio DSP nodes into self-contained formats, its web export pipeline generates standalone HTML widgets that require zero external dependencies, zero CDN requests, and zero script frameworks. Here is how these embeds are structured, how the microphone reactivity works, and how you can place one on any page with a standard iframe. The problem with traditional web audio visualisers Most web visualisers rely on heavy JavaScript libraries such as Three.js, Babylon.js, or complex bundling setups. When embedded inside an article or project portfolio, these libraries create three distinct friction points: Payload weight and cold starts : Loading megabyte-scale runtime libraries introduces layout shifts, slow paint times, and stuttering initial frames. Audio context locking : Modern web browsers block audio playback and microphone capture until an explicit user interaction occurs. If an embedded canvas tries to initialise WebAudio automatically, the browser mutes or rejects the audio stream. Cross-origin security restrictions : When hosting visual widgets in iframes, microphone access requires explicit permission delegation via the allow="microphone" attribute. Without this header, permission dialogues fail silently. Infinite solves this by generating single-file HTML embeds where the entire WebGL vertex shader, fragment shader, audio analysis loop, and fallback UI live in under twelve kilobytes of plain text. Keep reading . on this page The geometry of deterministic chaos Numerical integration and step resolution Real-time simulation in a Sketch node Audio-reactive modulation of system parameters Sonification and 3D visual geometry Creative workflows and live performance A Lorenz attractor interactive simulation brings the non-linear elegance of deterministic chaos into modern creative coding and live audiovisual performance. In traditional generative art, procedural movement often relies on periodic functions like sine waves or pseudorandom noise fields. While periodic functions offer predictable repetition and noise fields produce uncorrelated drifting, neither captures the natural tension of complex physical systems: structured form that evolves continuously without ever repeating. In modular workstations like Infinite , the Lorenz attractor bridges mathematics, real-time computer graphics, and modular sound design. By evaluating its three coupled differential equations inside a programmable canvas, artists can project intricate three-dimensional phase space paths, modulate attractor dynamics live with audio frequencies, and sonify chaotic coordinates into synthesiser parameters. Here is how the underlying non-linear mathematics work, how to implement the simulation inside a Sketch node, and how to patch chaotic variables across visual and audio nodes on a single canvas. Lorenz attractor interactive simulation diagram displaying differential equations, phase space trajectories, and modular node wiring The geometry of deterministic chaos The Lorenz system was introduced in 1963 by mathematician and meteorologist Edward Lorenz. While studying a simplified twelve-variable mathematical model of atmospheric convection, Lorenz reduced the convective fluid flow between warm lower and cool upper boundaries to a minimal system of three autonomous ordinary differential equations: dx / dt = sigma * (y - x) dy / dt = x * (rho - z) - y dz / dt = x * y - beta * z Here, the state variables describe idealized physical properties: x is proportional to the rate of convective fluid circulation. y is proportional to the horizontal temperature variation between ascending and descending currents. z measures the distortion of the vertical temperature profile from pure linearity. The three system parameters govern the physical regime: sigma (the Prandtl number) represents the ratio of kinematic viscosity to thermal diffusivity. In standard simulations, this is fixed at 10.0 . beta represents the geometric aspect ratio of the convective roll cells, traditionally set to 8.0 / 3.0 (approximately 2.667 ). rho (the Rayleigh number) measures the normalized temperature difference driving the fluid convection. It serves as the primary bifurcation parameter. When rho is less than 1.0 , the system has only one stable equilibrium at the coordinate origin (0, 0, 0) , representing pure conduction where fluid motion dissipates. As rho exceeds 1.0 , two symmetric convective fixed points emerge, labelled C+ and C- : C+, C- = (+-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), +-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), rho - 1) At the canonical threshold rho = 28.0 , both equilibrium points become unstable spirals. Instead of settling into a fixed point or a simple limit cycle, the trajectory enters bounded deterministic chaos. The path orbits one fixed point, spirals outward as its radius expands, and then crosses the saddle point at the origin to loop around the opposing lobe. Because the trajectory never intersects itself in three-dimensional phase space, it traces a fractal structure with a Hausdorff dimension of approximately 2.06 . Numerical integration and ste

You need Infinite and about ten minutes. No plugins or extra software. 1. Start from a template Open the Library and download Moves with the music . It is a small patch where a shape grows with the sound. Open the file from File, Open in Infinite and press play. A template is a normal patch, so everything in it can be changed. 2. Follow the cable The patch has two halves, and the template labels them with comments on the canvas. The sound. A Random Note Generator plays an Analog synth into Audio Out . The picture. A Shape goes through a Bloom effect to the Output node. What joins them is an Audio Analyze node. It listens to the sound and turns it into moving numbers: level, low, mid and high. Those numbers drive the shape's Size X and Size Y. Controls that are driven by the music show an orange dot. That is the whole trick. Any number can move any control. 3. Change what moves Try these one at a time: Switch the source of Size X from level to low or high . Low reacts to bass, high to the bright parts of the sound. Change the Depth of a driven control to make it move more or less. Raise the Intensity on Bloom for a stronger glow. Add an LFO and connect it to a colour control, so the picture drifts even when the music is quiet. 4. Bring your own sound Replace the template's synth with a Sampler or an audio file, or load a VST3 or AU plugin and play it from your MIDI keyboard. The Audio Analyze node listens to whatever you connect to it. 5. Save and share Patches are plain-text .inf files. Send the file to a friend and they get exactly your setup. Keep reading . on this page What you need The three nodes Smooth, hold and mirror Three patches to try Tips from how the trackers work Combine it with sound Try it Free motion tracking software is built into Infinite as an optional pack: it turns a camera image into numbers you can wire to anything: a shader's size, a filter cutoff, a synth note. There are three tracking nodes, Hand Track, Face Track and Pose Track, and each one outputs modulators the same way an LFO does. This post explains what they give you, how to set them up, and where they work well. What you need Infinite 0.5.0 or later. The free Tracking pack (26 MB). Open Settings, then Extensions, and press Install next to Tracking. It installs while the app runs, with no restart. If you are offline, download the pack for your platform from the Extensions page and use Install from file. A video source: a camera, a video file or a still image. The pack is optional on purpose. If you never track anything, you never download it. The three nodes All three live in the Modulators category. Each has a present output that says whether a subject was found, followed by the values below. Hand Track gives you palm x , palm y , index x , index y , thumb x , thumb y , then pinch , open , roll and size . It also has six gesture flags: fist , point , peace , thumbs up , ok and rock . Face Track gives you head x , head y , yaw , pitch and roll , then eye L , eye R , brows , mouth , smile , gaze x and gaze y . Pose Track gives you body x , body y , head x , head y , both wrists as wrist L x , wrist L y , wrist R x , wrist R y , then arm L , arm R , spread , lean and size . Because these are ordinary modulator outputs, you connect them the same way as any other: drag a modulation cable to a parameter. Nothing about the destination needs to know it is being driven by a body. Smooth, hold and mirror Raw tracking jitters, and a hand leaving the frame for a moment should not make a visual snap to zero. Each tracking node has three settings for this: mirror , on by default, so that moving your right hand moves things to the right on screen, like a mirror. smoothing , 0.5 by default. At 0 the values are raw. Towards 1 they are very smooth. The filter is speed adaptive (One-Euro), so slow movements are smoothed hard while fast movements stay responsive. holdMs , 150 by default. After the subject is lost, the node keeps the last values for that many milliseconds before reporting that nothing is there. The gesture flags and present skip the smoothing, since a gesture is either on or off. The node body shows a live landmark overlay and slider-style meters, so you can see what the tracker sees before you wire anything. Three patches to try A pinch that controls a filter. Add a Hand Track node, then wire pinch to a filter cutoff on a synth or a hosted plugin. Closing your fingers closes the filter. If you want a different range, put a Range to Range node between them. A head that steers the picture. Wire Face Track yaw and pitch to a shape's rotation or to a shader's offset, and smile to colour or brightness. For a gallery piece this is enough: a screen that leans towards the person looking at it. Arms as a conductor. Wire Pose Track arm L and arm R to two different parameters, for example the level of two instruments, and spread to the amount of an effect. Stand back from the camera so the whole upper body is in frame. Tips from how the trackers work Light the subject from the front. A bright window behind you makes the face and hands harder to find. Keep the whole hand in view. size tells you how close it is to the camera, which is a useful modulator on its own. Use the gesture flags as switches and the continuous outputs as knobs. One graph for sound and pictures: how Infinite syncs them
Infinite runs a pull-based audio graph and a GPU texture pipeline off one BPM transport, so audio can drive visuals and visuals can drive audio.

Two graphs, one clock . Modulation crosses the boundary . Why one canvas helps . Try it . Make something with it . Keep reading . on this page Two graphs, one clock Modulation crosses the boundary Why one canvas helps Try it Video tools and audio tools usually live in separate programs. You wire them together with OSC, MIDI clock or a texture-sharing protocol, and you accept a little latency and jitter on the way. Infinite takes a different route: audio and visuals are two parts of one engine that share a transport. Two graphs, one clock The engine has two sides, and each one follows the rules of its own medium. Audio is a pull-based, sample-accurate graph. If a buffer is late, you hear a click, so it is built around a deadline. Visuals are a GPU texture pipeline on GLSL and OpenGL 3.2 Core. A dropped frame is far less noticeable, but throughput matters. Both sides are tied to a global BPM transport, so a beat means the same moment in the sound and in the picture. Modulation crosses the boundary The useful part is what happens between the two. Any signal can modulate any control: an Audio Analyze node gives an 8-band FFT and onset detection; an LFO , Envelope Follower , Random or Pattern CV gives a moving number; an Image Analyze node reads luminance or motion from a picture. Wire the output of one of those to a control and it moves. That control can be a shader parameter, a 3D transform, a synth knob or the slider of a hosted plugin. Sound drives pictures, and pictures drive sound. Why one canvas helps When both live on the same canvas, the connection is a cable you can see. There is no second application to launch, no port to configure and no project that has to be kept in sync by hand. A patch is also a plain-text .inf file, so it can be versioned, diffed and rendered without a window . Try it Open the Moves with the music template from the Library . It is a shape that grows with the sound, and it is the smallest example of the idea above. Breakdown of Infinite register machine for Field Synth and Effect nodes, compiling per-sample audio DSP kernels at 48kHz.

Keep reading . on this page How the sample register machine works A 1-pole lowpass filter kernel Shipped Moog 4-pole ladder filter Real-time mod matrix integration Testing and verifying headlessly Most modern digital audio workstations treat audio synthesis as a black box: you write a C++ plugin, compile a VST3 or AU bundle with JUCE or Dplug, restart your host, and attach a debugger. In Infinite, you can write audio DSP at the sample level directly inside the canvas using Field language . Your code runs on the audio thread once per sample (48,000 times per second), compiled to a register machine that executes with zero memory allocations. How the sample register machine works When you place a Field Synth ( Synths Field Synth ) or Field Effect ( AudioEffects Field Effect ) node, Infinite compiles the kernel expression to a compact bytecode representation that evaluates on register cells. Built-in variables available on the audio thread sr : Audio sample rate in Hz (typically 48000.0 ). in : Incoming audio sample value ( [-1.0, 1.0] ) in Field Effect. out : Output audio sample to write. freq : Note frequency in Hz (voice pitch in Field Synth). gate : 1.0 while a MIDI note is held down, 0.0 when released. noteVel : Key velocity ( [0.0, 1.0] ). state : Declares per-voice persistent memory preserved across samples. param : Exposes a modulatable float knob on the node body with min/max bounds. A 1-pole lowpass filter kernel Here is a classic 1-pole lowpass filter written in 4 lines: param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99] state float z = 0 z += (in - z) * cutoff out = z Because state float z = 0 allocates a persistent cell in the voice register, z retains its previous sample value, creating an analog RC filter response. Shipped Moog 4-pole ladder filter For aggressive saturation and self-oscillation, Infinite ships with a 4-pole cascaded non-linear filter: param float cutoff = 2200.0 [80.0, 14000.0] param float res = 0.70 [0.0, 0.98] param float drive = 1.50 [1.0, 4.0] param float mix = 1.0 [0.0, 1.0] state float s1 = 0 state float s2 = 0 state float s3 = 0 state float s4 = 0 f = clamp((cutoff / sr) * 2.2, 0.005, 0.42) feedback = (s4 * res * 3.6) / (1.0 + abs(s4) * 0.8) u = (in * drive) - feedback sat = u / (1.0 + abs(u) * 0.3) s1 = s1 + f * (sat - s1) s2 = s2 + f * (s1 - s2) s3 = s3 + f * (s2 - s3) s4 = s4 + f * (s3 - s4) wet = s4 out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix Notice the dry/wet mix pattern at the end: every Field audio effect ends with out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix , giving you instant parallel processing. Real-time mod matrix integration Unlike fixed DSP plugins, a Field Effect node can publish meter readings back to the visual and modulation canvas using reduce.rms : param float boost = 1.5 [0.5, 4.0] output frame float bass = reduce.rms(in, 20.0, 200.0) out = in * boost The bass scalar automatically becomes a second output pin on the node. You can run a cable from that pin directly into a 3D geometry deformer, a light intensity slider, or a GLSL shader. Testing and verifying headlessly You can test Field kernels without opening the GUI using Infinite's CLI or Python SDK: import infinite # Synthesize a custom per-sample subtractive saw voice infinite.field_synth(""" state float phase = 0 phase = (phase + freq / sr) % 1.0 out = (phase * 2.0 - 1.0) * 0.3 * gate """, out_wav="saw.wav", duration=3) The CLI synthesizes the audio, measures integrated LUFS, checks for clipped frames, and writes the output file with zero GUI dependencies. your turn Make something with it Infinite is free and open source for macOS, Windows and Linux. Keep reading . on this page 1. generating base procedural meshes 2. deforming vertex topology with field modifier 3. connecting the audio-reactive graph 4. headless command-line rendering in traditional 3d software, generating complex procedural geometry requires heavy dcc suites like blender or houdini. when you want to connect that geometry to low-latency audio analysis, midi clocks, or live synthesis, you are forced into fragile websocket bridges or osc pipelines. infinite brings 3d geometry generation, vertex shading, and per-sample audio dsp onto the same unified execution graph. you can generate procedural vertex topologies, deform them with fast simd-vectorized field modifier kernels, and render them in real time at 60+ fps. 1. generating base procedural meshes infinite includes native parametric mesh generators: mesh cube : generates subdivisions with uv coordinates and normal vectors. mesh sphere : uv sphere or icosphere with customisable geodesic resolution. mesh torus : toroidal coordinates with major and minor radii controls. mesh grid : high-density planar vertex grid ideal for terrain and landscape deformation. each mesh node outputs a geometry buffer containing position ( vec3 pos ), normal ( vec3 norm ), texture coordinates ( vec2 uv ), and vertex colour ( vec4 color ). 2. deforming vertex topology with field modifier the field modifier node ( Filter FieldModifier ) accepts any input geometry and executes an inline field expression across every vertex in parallel. unlike traditional vertex shaders which only run during the gpu rasterization pass, field modifier runs directly on the engine's geometry data structure, allowing the resulting deformed mesh to be used for physics collisions, camera raycasting, or further topological operations. example: spherical ripple displacement driven by audio bass // inputs: pos (vec3), norm (vec3), uv (vec2), t (float), bass (float) let dist = length(pos) let freq = 6.0 let wave = sin(dist * freq - t * 4.0) * (0.15 + 0.4 * bass) let displaced_pos = pos + norm * wave out.pos = displaced_pos out.norm = normalize(norm + vec3(wave * 0.2, wave * 0.2, 0.0)) out.color = vec4(0.2 + 0.8 * bass, 0.4, 1.0 - wave, 1.0) in this single kernel: length(pos) calculates the distance from the mesh origin. norm * wave displaces vertices along their surface normals. bass scales the displacement amplitude in direct synchronization with your music's low-frequency energy. out.color generates dynamic vertex gradients without needing external texture maps. 3. connecting the audio-reactive graph wiring this up in infinite takes under thirty seconds: drop an audio file or synth node into the canvas. wire its output to an audio analyze node. wire the bass pin of audio analyze to the bass input of your field modifier . feed the deformed mesh output into a render 3d node equipped with a camera, ambient occlusion, and directional light. you now have a living, breathing 3d visualizer completely locked to your rhythm. 4. headless command-line rendering because infinite features a complete headless engine, you do not even need to open the graphical user interface to render 3d animations. you can execute high-resolution 4k video renders straight from your shell or an automated script: # render 10 seconds of 3d audio-reactive visuals to an mp4 file at 60 fps infinite export-video --graph project.json --audio track.wav --out visual.mp4 --fps 60 --width 1920 --height 1080 this makes infinite ideal for generative nft pipelines, music video automation, and automated social visual teasers. your turn Make something with it Infinite is free and open source for macOS, Windows and Linux. Render video and audio from a text file with no window open
Infinite's headless mode turns a plain-text patch into stills, video and a loudness report from the command line. Here is the five-minute workflow.

What you need . A complete patch in a dozen lines . Validate, draw, render . Ask the engine, do not guess . Measure the sound . Reading the result . Where this is useful . Make something with it . Keep reading . on this page What you need A complete patch in a dozen lines Validate, draw, render Ask the engine, do not guess Measure the sound Reading the result Where this is useful A headless DAW is one that renders with no window open. Most DAWs and visual tools only run with a window and a mouse. Infinite's engine does not need either. The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool, so a patch can be validated, drawn and rendered from a terminal, a script or a CI job. This post walks through the loop from the Headless User Guide : describe, write, validate, explain, look and listen, render. What you need The Infinite app. There is no separate package; the executable inside the app is the tool. A machine with working OpenGL, because frames are drawn by the real GPU pipeline. On Linux, a virtual display. Run each render as xvfb-run -a Infinite ... . A text editor. Patches are plain text files ending in .inf . Patches that use a camera, microphone or MIDI device are refused in headless mode (exit code 4), since there is no hardware to read. Swap them for a file or a generator. A complete patch in a dozen lines Save this as hello.inf : infinite-patch 1 node 1 Source Shape id shape i shapeType Star end node 2 Modulators LFO id lfo end node 3 Utility Output id out end cable out 0 shape mod shape sizeX lfo 0 0 1 0.5 expr shape rotation sin(t) * 90 That is one shape, one LFO and an output. The LFO drives the shape's width, and an expression spins it. Validate, draw, render Infinite --validate hello.inf Infinite --frame hello.inf 0,1,2 pics/ --contact-sheet sheet.png Infinite --render hello.inf hello.mp4 --duration 4 --fps 30 --validate loads the file strictly and lists every problem with its line number. --frame draws stills at 0, 1 and 2 seconds plus one labelled contact sheet. --render writes the video. Ask the engine, do not guess Two commands save a lot of trial and error: Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with their defaults, ranges and dropdown options. Infinite --explain hello.inf prints the graph that was actually built, so you can check every wire. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch. Measure the sound --audio-summary describes the audio as numbers: loudness, peaks, clipping, silence, a spectrum and a tempo guess. Infinite --audio-summary hello.inf summary.json --wav out.wav --duration 4 Add --stems id,id --stems-dir dir to write one WAV per named node, or --output node to measure a single Audio Out instead of the whole mix. Reading the result The last line printed is always one JSON object with ok , mode , frames , fps , size , audio , elapsed_ms , files , warnings and errors . A script can parse that line and branch on ok without scraping log text. Where this is useful Regression tests for sound and picture. Render a corpus of patches on every commit and compare the summaries. Batch exports. Produce a hundred variations of a piece from one patch with --set node.param=value . Bots and servers. Take a patch from a chat message and send back a video. Want to see what a patch looks like before scripting it? Start with the first steps tutorial . Shadertoy GLSL shaders in Infinite, made audio-reactive
How to convert any Shadertoy fragment shader into a native real-time node in Infinite, hook it up to audio analysis FFT bands, and export high-resolution video.

The coordinate space mapping . Adding instant audio reactivity . Live interactive WebGL widget . Exporting high-resolution video headlessly . Explore more embeds . Make something with it . Keep reading . on this page The coordinate space mapping Adding instant audio reactivity Live interactive WebGL widget Exporting high-resolution video headlessly Explore more embeds Shadertoy is the world's greatest sketchbook for pixel shaders. But getting a Shadertoy shader to respond dynamically to your music, sync with MIDI, or render out to high-resolution MP4 video often involves clumsy workarounds, browser recording extensions, or complex OSC bridges. In Infinite, shaders are native first-class nodes that sit directly alongside polyphonic synthesizers, audio effects, and sequencers on one infinite canvas. The coordinate space mapping Shadertoy uses standard pixel coordinates: void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) { vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy; // ... } In Infinite's Field Pixel node ( Source FieldPixel ), coordinates are normalized and aspect-corrected by default: uv : normalized texture coordinate ( [0, 1] x [0, 1] ) aspect : screen width divided by screen height ( res.x / res.y ) t : elapsed time in seconds (equivalent to iTime ) p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect : centre-origin aspect-corrected coordinates Adding instant audio reactivity On Shadertoy, audio reactivity requires binding an audio texture input ( iChannel0 ). In Infinite, audio reactivity is immediate and native: Wire an Audio Analyze node to your incoming sound or synth output. The node exposes 8 spectral bands: sub-bass, bass, low-mid, mid, high-mid, presence, brilliance, and onset pulses. Wire any band pin directly into a parameter on your Field Pixel shader node. Here is an authentic audio-reactive neon tunnel kernel in Field language: p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect; r = length(p); a = atan(p.y, p.x); u_coord = a / 3.14159265; v_coord = 1.0 / (r + 0.001) + t * (1.5 + 1.2 * bass); grid_u = abs(fract(u_coord * 4.0) - 0.5); grid_v = abs(fract(v_coord * 2.0) - 0.5); lines = smoothstep(0.42, 0.49, max(grid_u, grid_v)); wire = vec3(lines) * vec3(0.1, 0.85, 1.0) * (0.8 + 0.6 * mid); center = vec3(0.95, 0.2, 0.6) * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.6, r)) * (0.8 + 0.8 * bass); col = (wire + center) * (0.7 + 0.5 * bass); Live interactive WebGL widget You can test this exact visualizer running live in WebGL below: powered by infinite by naman soni Exporting high-resolution video headlessly Unlike web tools that drop frames during screen capture, Infinite renders every single frame deterministically through its headless C++ engine: # Render a 1080p 60fps MP4 video with synced 24-bit audio ./Infinite --render /path/to/shader_patch.inf output.mp4 --duration 10 --fps 60 Every frame is rendered offscreen using OpenGL 3.2 framebuffers, guaranteeing zero dropped frames even on complex raymarchers. CHAPTER 01 What Field is, and why it exists Infinite is a node-based

CHAPTER 01 What Field is, and why it exists Infinite is a node-based audiovisual workstation: you build patches by wiring boxes together on a canvas. Most boxes do one fixed thing. Field is different. It is a small text language that lets you write what a box does, instead of picking from a menu. The one idea underneath all of Field is the kernel: a short body of code run once per element of some domain, automatically, forever. Write col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5) and it runs once per pixel, 60 times a second, on the GPU: a shader. Write P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 and it runs once per point in a mesh: a geometry deformer. Write out = in * 0.5 and it runs once per audio sample: a DSP effect. You never say where it runs; Field infers that from which identifiers your code touches. Every example in this manual is valid, runnable Field code written against the six node types that ship in Infinite today. Chapter 13 covers the language additions that landed after v1. CHAPTER 02 The five domains A domain is "what counts as one element." Four of the five map to real Field node types. The fifth, frame , has no node of its own. DOMAIN RUNS HOSTED BY PRODUCES graph once, at edit time Field Graph mounts and wires other real Infinite nodes frame once per rendered frame (about 60 a hoisted inside any of the other four, for one value shared across all elements second) shared values that frame element once per point or vertex per frame Field Modifier, Field Primitive mesh or point-cloud geometry and per-point colour pixel once per pixel per frame, on the GPU Field Pixel a 2D texture sample once per audio sample per voice Field Effect, Field Synth an audio signal (48,000 a second) The domain lattice This is the shape that governs what can see what. element , pixel and sample are mutually incomparable peers: an element kernel cannot read a pixel or sample value directly, in either direction. The only way to move a value between them is up through frame and bac
CHAPTER 03 Core syntax Field reads like a small C-family language.

CHAPTER 03 Core syntax Field reads like a small C-family language. Here is everything that is not obvious from that alone. Bare names, no sigil Every identifier, whether a reserved name like P , uv , in , out or your own param , state and attrib names, is written bare, exactly like a normal variable. Unlike Houdini VEX's @P style, Field has no sigil at all. P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2 Types and swizzles The type keywords are float , int , bool , vec2 , vec3 , vec4 . There is no string type inside a kernel body. Swizzles work like GLSL: .x .y .z .w and .r .g .b .a , one to four letters. The two letter sets do not mix in one swizzle ( .xg is not valid; use .xy or .rg ). Operators, comments and broadcast Arithmetic is + - * / % , comparison is < <= > >= == != , boolean is && || ! , and ^ is exponentiation ( a ^ b is pow(a, b) ), not XOR. There are no bitwise operators. // starts a line comment. A scalar auto-broadcasts against a vector: P += 0.1 adds to every component, with no vec3(0
CHAPTER 04 Declarations: attrib, param, state Three keywords cover

CHAPTER 04 Declarations: attrib, param, state Three keywords cover everything a kernel needs to remember or expose: a per-element scratch value, a UI knob, and a value that reads back one cycle late. attrib: a value that lives per element Declares a per-element scratch value, initialized once. Whatever you assign into it that frame is what the rest of the kernel body sees. Element domain only. attrib float heat = 0 heat = (P.y + 1.0) * 0.5 Cd = vec3(heat, 0.2, 1.0 - heat) An element attribute ramp driving vertex colour. param: a value that becomes a UI knob param <type> <name> = <default> [<lo>, <hi>] declares a real, modulatable knob. It shows up on the node's faceplate, can be dragged, automated and cabled to a modulator. param float speed = 2.0 [0.1, 10.0] Punctuation: in pixel kernels every statement ends with a semicolon ( param float speed = 2.0 [0.1, 10.0]; ). In element and sample kernels, statements are newline-terminated with no semicolon. state: this frame reads last frame's

CHAPTER 07 Randomness rand , noise and sh are pure functions of their

CHAPTER 07 Randomness rand , noise and sh are pure functions of their arguments: same inputs, same output, always, so a kernel stays deterministic and re-runnable. There is no hidden global RNG state to seed or reset. rand(min, max, speed, seed) Takes 0 to 4 arguments; fewer arguments fall back to sane defaults. n = rand(0, 1, 2.0, 0) P += N * (n - 0.5) * 0.2 Normal displacement using smooth noise: 0 to 1, speed 2.0, seed 0. noise and sh noise and sh follow the same pure-function pattern as rand , taking 0 to 4 arguments. Reach for rand first for most device work; use noise or sh when you want a smoother or shaped variant and want to compare results by ear or eye. FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL INFINITE / FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL
CHAPTER 08 Building a device There are two ways to bundle Field

CHAPTER 08 Building a device There are two ways to bundle Field kernels into something that behaves like one reusable device, rather than a single raw kernel box. 1. Single-node dynamic pins Any element, pixel or sample kernel can declare extra pins right in its code (up to 16 combined input and output pins per kernel): output frame float glow = abs(sin(t * speed)) This creates a real extra pin on the canvas node that can be wired with a cable, saves and loads with the patch, and survives undo. It is the cheapest way to add a second domain's worth of I/O to a device that is really one native node's behaviour. What a declared output pin carries today: a fixed value of 0. For a value that genuinely reaches another node right now, read it off one of the node's built-in toggle outputs instead: rms on Field Effect and Field Synth, publish on Field Modifier and Field Primitive, or state on Field Pixel. Use a hand-declared output pin when you want the pin present and wired for later, and one
CHAPTER 09 Field node reference Field is exposed to the user as six

CHAPTER 09 Field node reference Field is exposed to the user as six node types, each hosting one domain's kernel. All six compile the same source-text grammar covered in Chapters 1 to 8; the only thing that changes is which reserved names are in scope and which backend the kernel is compiled to. NODE DOMAIN WHAT IT DOES Field element Runs a per-vertex kernel over geometry already on the canvas, modifying P , N , uv , Cd and custom Modifier attributes. Field element Generates procedural point geometry from scratch, with no input required, using a per-element kernel (Circle, Primitive Spiral, Grid Lattice, Fibonacci Sphere, Helix and Torus Knot presets as starting points). Field sample Runs a kernel once per audio sample, on the audio thread. in is the audio input pin, state declares per- Effect voice memory, param exposes a knob, and reduce.rms(in, loHz, hiHz) publishes a band-limited RMS reading once per block. Field sample A polyphonic, note-driven synthesizer using the same sample-do

CHAPTER 10 Device faceplate Every Field node has two views: a compact

CHAPTER 10 Device faceplate Every Field node has two views: a compact body on the canvas, and a separate editor window for the code. The compact node body shows the auto-generated param knobs, notice text and an "Edit Field..." button. No source code is visible here. The floating editor window, opened by "Edit Field...", is where you read and write the kernel's text, inspect compilation status and see a live preview. What the faceplate gives you Knob rows laid out on Infinite's standard grid, so a Field node's knobs look and behave like every other node's, even with a variable-length, user-authored param list. An inline preview in the compact body: a live texture thumbnail on Field Pixel, a live scope on Field Effect and Field Synth, and a mini-viewport on Field Modifier and Field Primitive. Device save, import and export controls inside the editor window, so you can manage device files without closing the code view. FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL INFINITE / FIELD LANGUAGE MANUAL
CHAPTER 11 Saving and sharing devices: .infdev Field devices save and

CHAPTER 11 Saving and sharing devices: .infdev Field devices save and load through a portable file format: plain JSON. { "format": "infdev", "version": 1, "meta": { "name": "My Device", "author": "you", "description": "optional", "domain": "element" }, "device": { "code": "param float amp = 0.8 [0.0, 3.0]\n...", "params": { "amp": 0.8 }, "nodeSettings": { "maxElements": 65536, "generateCount": 64 } } } nodeSettings differs per domain: a Field Primitive device carries maxElements and, when it has no upstream input, generateCount . BEFORE YOU START What even is Infinite? Infinite is a node-based studio for making sound and image at the same time. Instead of separate apps for music, visuals, and 3D, you drop blocks called nodes onto one canvas and connect them with cables: a synth feeding a filter, a shape feeding a kaleidoscope, a drumbeat feeding a bouncing particle field. Because everything lives on the same clock, sound and image can react to each other in real time: a kick drum can punch a shape, a camera's motion can bend a synth's pitch, a color can become a chord. There is no "render and wait". You hear and see the result the instant you plug a cable in. This guide walks through every node in Infinite's palette, 333 spawnable node types, including the 34-filter image effects shelf and the 20-effect audio shelf. Halftone Recreates the image using a grid of dots sized by brightness

Source The node that produces the control signal: macro xy, random, an LFO, an envelope and so on. Destination The node that receives it. Parameter Which parameter on the destination is being moved. Value The live, current value of that parameter after modulation. Confidence Used by prediction sources to report how sure they are. It shows -- for ordinary sources. Lo / Hi The range the parameter travels between. Click a number to type an exact limit. Narrow it for subtle movement. Inv Inverts the mapping: when the source goes up, the parameter goes down. Curve The response curve between source and parameter, drawn as a small graph. Signal A tiny live scope of the incoming signal, so you can see it moving. x Removes the route.
